analysis.one_liner: Strips federal interest and depreciation tax deductions from landlords owning 50 or more single-family rental homes.
analysis.headline: Two House Democrats introduced the HOMES Act in July 2025; it has sat in the Ways and Means Committee since referral, with one cosponsor and no committee vote or floor action.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill changes the tax code so that any taxpayer who owns 50 or more single-family rental properties — large corporate and institutional landlords — can no longer deduct mortgage interest or depreciation on those properties. Tax law lets investors deduct the cost of borrowing and the wear-and-tear on buildings, which lowers what large owners pay in taxes. The bill keeps those deductions for owners with fewer than 50 homes, for low-income housing tax credit properties, for newly built rentals, and it restores the deductions if a large owner sells a home to an individual buyer who will live in it or to certain affordable-housing nonprofits [S2] [S3].
analysis.who_benefits: Renters and first-time homebuyers in markets where large investors have bought up single-family homes. Large owners would face higher after-tax costs on homes they hold for rent, which raises the price of selling to an individual owner-occupant instead — a sale that restores the deduction in the year of sale [S2] [S3]. Owners with fewer than 50 properties keep their deductions, so small and individual landlords become relatively better positioned against large competitors [S3].

how_it_helps.text: Denies interest and depreciation deductions to any taxpayer owning 50 or more single-family rental properties, defined with aggregation rules that count commonly controlled entities as one owner so the threshold cannot be dodged by splitting ownership across companies [S3] [S2].
Preserves the deductions only for homes with low-income housing tax credits and for newly built rentals, so the bill targets owners of existing housing rather than new supply [S2].

Restores the deduction in the year a property is sold if the buyer is an individual using it as a principal residence or a qualified nonprofit, community land trust, land bank, or public housing agency subsidiary — steering large owners toward selling homes to people who will live in them [S3] [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Large corporate and institutional owners of single-family rental homes, who would pay higher taxes on portfolios of 50 or more small residential rental properties; the bill directs the Treasury to write rules preventing avoidance [S2] [S3].

drawbacks.text: Higher tax costs on large rental owners could be passed through to tenants as higher rents, since the owners of existing rental homes are the ones who set asking rents; the bill raises their costs of holding homes for rent [S3].

The bill does not change what these owners may charge tenants; it changes only their tax treatment, so any benefit to renters depends on large owners choosing to sell rather than absorb the higher tax bill [S2] [S3].

The 50-property threshold and the carve-outs for new construction and low-income tax credit properties mean much of the institutional market — large apartment buildings and newly built rental subdivisions — is untouched; the bill reaches only a slice of the rental market [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill attacks a real tax advantage that favors the largest owners of existing single-family homes, and its sale-to-occupant provision is a direct push toward homeownership. But it is a blunt and narrow tool: it does not cap rents, does not cover most large apartment buildings or new construction, and its benefit to renters rests entirely on assumptions about how large owners will respond to higher tax costs. As written it is a modest, targeted change, not a broad affordability fix.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee in July 2025 and no further action has been taken on it.

narrative.text: Rep. Emilia Sykes introduced the HOMES Act in the House on July 10, 2025, joined by one cosponsor, Rep. Summer Lee of Pennsylvania [S1] [S3] [S4].
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means the same day, and the action record shows no markup, hearing, vote, or floor action since [S5] [S1].
Congress remains in session until January 2027, so the bill is technically alive but has sat untouched in committee for months [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large corporate owners of single-family rental homes are better off so far: the tax deductions the bill would deny them remain fully in place because the bill has not moved in committee. Renters and homebuyers gain nothing yet either; the bill is simply stalled.

for.name: Rep. Emilia Strong Sykes
for.what_they_did: Introduced the HOMES Act on July 10, 2025 to deny interest and depreciation deductions to owners of 50 or more single-family rental properties [S1] [S3].

for.name: Rep. Summer Lee
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, the only cosponsor in the record [S4].

against.name: Rep. Jason Smith
against.role: Chair, House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after its referral to the Ways and Means Committee; no markup or vote has been scheduled in the months since introduction [S5].

sides.party_line_note: The bill was introduced and cosponsored by two House Democrats with no Republican support in the record, and no vote has ever been taken, so the partisan shape of the broader House is unknown.

industries.industry: Large corporate and institutional owners of single-family rental homes
industries.note: These owners profit from tax deductions on borrowing and building depreciation; the bill removes those deductions on portfolios of 50 or more small rental properties. Their interest in keeping the deductions runs against renters' interest in seeing the homes sold to occupants, since the deduction is only restored when a home is sold to a resident owner [S3] [S2].

Owners with fewer than 50 properties keep all their deductions, giving them a tax advantage relative to large competitors; to the extent small landlords compete with large investors for homes, renters benefit too [S3].

industries.industry: Homebuilders and developers of newly built rental housing
industries.note: Newly constructed rentals are exempt from the deduction ban, making new building relatively more attractive than buying existing homes; the bill thus nudges capital toward construction rather than acquisition of existing stock [S2].
Properties eligible for the low-income housing tax credit are exempt from the deduction ban, keeping the existing tax-credit channel as a protected route for affordable rental housing [S2].

analysis.trajectory: With a single cosponsor and no committee action for months, the bill's realistic path is to die in the Ways and Means Committee when this Congress ends in January 2027, unless advocates build substantially more cosponsor support or attach the provision to a broader tax bill.
